translations.text: A discourse of our holy father Basil on humility
Man ought to have remained in the glory given by God, and to have had a height that was true and not contrived,
when he was made strong by the power of God, shone with divine wisdom, and rejoiced in eternal good.
But since he exchanged that desire for divine glory and began to seek something greater, which he could not attain, he therefore lost even what he had the power to hold.
Now therefore the good life, the remedy for this sickness of his, and what turns him back to his former honor is humility, and,
that he should not seek vain glory, but should ask for glory from God.
For in this way he may correct his error, in this way he may heal his sickness, in this way he may return to that first commandment.
But the devil, who made people fall through the hope of that false glory,
does not cease from tempting them, and he seeks every means to this end, and he makes an abundance of riches appear great to a person, so that all his zeal may be directed toward it.
Yet this is no glory at all, but rather a great ruin.
For the acquisition of riches is a work of greed, and it is of no use for glory; rather it blinds a person to no purpose, exalts him emptily, and makes him like those who are swollen.
For just as swollen people are not so thick because of health and good bodily condition, but because of many diseases, so too is arrogance in the soul.
For there are people who are proud not only of wealth, of the laying of splendid tables, of the beauty of their clothing, and of their multitude of slaves and servants,
but who also exalt themselves over honors given by others.
If they become rulers of a people, or receive some other honor, they are proud, as though they had become higher than human nature,
and they exalt themselves as if mounted upon the clouds, and they regard the people beneath them as fit to be trampled on; and those from whom they have received
honor are the very ones against whom they rage, and those through whom they are proud are the very ones they despise, and they do a thing full of folly.
For they have a glory feebler than a dream, and they are clothed in a splendor emptier than the shadows of the night,
for it is created by a nod of the people and by a nod it comes to an end, as with that foolish son of Solomon,
a child in age and more childish still in mind, whom the people asked for gentler leadership, and he threatened them with harsher; and thus by that very deed
by which he thought he would appear mighty, he was utterly driven out of the kingship.
A person is also puffed up by strength of body, swiftness of feet, and beauty of youthful stature.
which are things that can be destroyed by diseases and wasted away by time. And they do not know that:
"All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass."
The grass withers and the flower falls." Such were the boastings of the giants over their strength:
and the foolish mind of Goliath, who fought against God, and Adonijah, puffed up over his beauty, and Absalom, who boasted of the loveliness of his hair.
But that which among men is reckoned great and firm above all else, namely wisdom and philosophy,
its loftiness too is truly vain if it is merely fleshly and divine wisdom is not joined to it, and it is reckoned as nothing.
For, first of all, the devil himself is more skilled than anyone in the wisdom of the world, and he went astray in that skill of his.
And the scheme that he devised against man, by which he deceived him with that evil wisdom of his, turned out to the harm of his own self,
for by it he fell away from God completely and was condemned to eternal death.
Yet he could not cast man away from God completely, but he himself fell away; and again, in the snare that he set for the Lord, he himself was caught;
and he who thought to harm the Lord through the crucifixion was himself harmed by his crucifixion; and by the death with which he wished to kill the Lord, he himself died.
So then, if the ruler of this world, the first, great and invisible teacher of that vain wisdom, falls by his own wisdom and arrives at the utmost foolishness,
how much more do his disciples and those who resemble him become fools, even though they think themselves wise.
For see how Pharaoh wished by his wisdom to wipe out the people of Israel, but that scheme of his turned to his own grief, from a quarter where he did not expect it.
And the infant who had been given over to death by his command was brought up in his own royal house, and he did not realize
how in his own house was being raised his destroyer, the one who would lead out all the people of Israel.
And the murderer Abimelech, the illegitimate son of Gideon, who slaughtered his seventy legitimate sons and thought
that he had done something wise, so that he might hold the kingship firmly, in the end struck down those
who had become helpers in that evil of his, and afterward destroyed them [?], by the hand of a woman and the throwing of a stone.
And the Jews too devised, as wisdom, that evil counsel against the Lord, when they said:
"If we leave him alone, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and lay waste our land and our nation."
By this counsel they became murderers of Christ, in order to save their land.
And they perished by that counsel and were taken captive from that land and became strangers to the law and the temple.
And so, in many ways, a person can find, if he looks for it, how vain the business of human wisdom is.
And it is lowly and small, rather than lofty and great.
And no one who has sense would be puffed up over wisdom or any other good thing of his own.
Rather, let him listen to the good teaching of the blessed Hannah, and again of the prophet Jeremiah, which says:
"Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches; but what is the true boast, and by what deed does a man become great?
"In this let him boast," it says, "whoever boasts: in the understanding and knowledge of the Lord."
This is the height of man, this is his glory and might: that he should recognize the true glory and seek glory from the Lord, the only glorious one, as the Apostle says:
"Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." For "Christ has become for us wisdom from God, wholeness and holiness and redeemer."
For this is the perfect and good boasting in the Lord: that no one should exalt himself either over his own righteousness or over any accomplishment,
but should recognize how he falls short of the true righteousness and is justified only by faith in Christ,
just as Paul boasts of his contempt for his own righteousness and of his seeking the righteousness that comes through Christ,
which is from God, and of faith in the knowledge of him and the power of his resurrection, and of sharing in his sufferings,
being conformed to his death, so that he may attain the resurrection of the dead.
Here, then, all the height of pride has fallen, and no pretext for arrogance is left to you, O man,
whose boast and hope lie in this: that you put yourself to death to every deed and be saved through Christ for that future life,
the beginning of which we have here, we who are saved entirely by the grace and gift of God.
For it is God "who gives us the will and the doing of good," and it is God who his own wisdom, ordained beforehand,
reveals to us for our glory through his Spirit, and it is God who gives us strength in our labor, as the Apostle says:
"I labored more than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of God that was with me." And it is God too who delivers us from trials, as it is said:
"We ourselves had received within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we should not trust in ourselves but in God,
who raises the dead, who delivered us from so great a death and delivers us, in whom we hope that he will deliver us yet again, with the help of your prayers."
Why then are you proud, as though of your own achievements, of these things granted to you by God, for which you owe thanks to the Giver? For:
"What do you have that you have not received? And if you have received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it from another," but had it of yourself?
You did not come to know God by your righteousness, but God knew you because of his goodness, for: we have known God, and rather we are known by God.
It is not that you found Christ by your virtue, but Christ found you by his coming, for it says:
"I press on, so that I may lay hold of that for which Christ laid hold of me," as the Lord says:
"You did not choose me, but I chose you." But you, because you have been honored, are you proud because of this?
And do you take the mercy that was shown to you as a reason for arrogance?
But you will know yourself, who you are, at that time when you are driven out, like Adam from Paradise, and are abandoned,
as when the Spirit of God abandoned Saul, and as when Israel was cut off from the holy root.
"Do not, then, exalt yourself, for you stand by faith; rather, be afraid, for judgment follows grace, and how you make use of what has been granted to you, this the Judge will examine.
But if you have not understood even this, that whatever you have, you have by the grace of God,
but instead you call what was given by him your own, as something acquired by your own strength, then in the face of such excessive ignorance I no longer know what to say to you.
Or do you not know that you are not more honorable than the blessed apostle Peter?
For you do not even have as much love for God as he did, who loved him so much that he eagerly desired death for his sake and said to him:
"Even if all stumble because of you, I will never stumble."
But since he had said this word boastfully, he was therefore given over to human fear and fell into denial,
so that in this way, through that error, he might learn not to trust in himself and also to have mercy on the weak.
For he too received experience of that human weakness and understood that, just as when he was sinking in the sea
he was made firm by the right hand of the Lord, so too in that sea of stumbling, when he came close to drowning through unbelief,
he was kept safe by the power of Christ, who had told him everything beforehand: "Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times."
And in this way the Lord rightly reproved Peter and helped him, so that he might thus learn humility and mercy toward the weak.
But that Pharisee, boastful and arrogant, who not only boasted about himself
but also disparaged the tax collector before God, in this way destroyed his boast of righteousness through the evil of arrogance.
And the tax collector went down justified rather than he, for he glorified the holy and good Lord and did not even dare to look up, but asked only for mercy.
And he was his own accuser by the manner of his standing and by the beating of his breast, and because he asked for nothing else but mercy alone.
Now, therefore, look at this example and beware of the evil of arrogance, as it came upon that Pharisee.
And he came to be in want of righteousness [?]; by his arrogance he destroyed his own grace, and through that boasting he became lower than that humble man and sinner,
since he exalted himself above him and did not wait for God's judgment, but passed judgment by his own will.
But do not exalt yourself over any person, even if he is more sinful than all sinners, for humility often delivers one who has greatly offended from his sins.
And therefore I say to you: do not justify yourself above another, lest you be justified by your own judgment and condemned by God's, as the great apostle Paul says:
"I do not judge myself, for I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not justified by this; the one who justifies me is the Lord."
And now you too, if you think that you have done some good, give thanks to God and do not exalt yourself over your neighbor, as it is written:
"Let each one examine his own work, and then he will have his boast in himself and not in regard to another."
For how have you benefited your neighbor if you have confessed the faith, or endured persecution for the name of the Lord, or borne the labors of fasting?
That [?] benefit is not another's, but your own.
Be afraid of resembling the fall of the devil, who exalted himself over man, and then fell through man and was given over to be trampled by the very one he had trampled.
Such also was the fall of the Israelites, for they exalted themselves over the gentiles,
as over the unclean, and they themselves became more unclean, and their righteousness became like the rag of a menstruating woman,
while the defilement and uncleanness of the gentiles was wiped away by faith.
Remember, then, the saying of Solomon, which he speaks above all else:
"The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." And again, keep in your heart the saying of the Lord himself, in which he says:
"Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted."
Do not be an unjust judge of yourself, nor pass judgment on yourself with partiality, so that if you had something good, you would look only at that and willingly forget your sins.
Do not do this: exalting yourself over some good thing you have just now done, while forgiving yourself the errors you committed this morning or yesterday.
Rather, when you do something good and it makes you elated, recall your former errors, so that in this way the foolish thought may subside.
And again, if you see a neighbor's error, do not judge him on that and look only at that, but recall also his virtues, both those you know and those that are not known to you,
for perhaps you will find him [?] to be far better than you, if only you examine everything and do not speak only of the error and no longer of the good.
For God does not judge people on one side only, as it is written:
"I am coming to gather their deeds and their thoughts." And again, when he was angry with Jehoshaphat for his sin of that time,
he also recalled his good deeds and said, "Good words have been found in you."
This and all such things let us say to ourselves, in order to root pride out of us, and let us always humble ourselves, so that in this way we may be exalted.
Let us become like the Lord who came down from heaven, who came to the utmost humility, so that in this way we too may be exalted through humility.
For we find that all the deeds of the Lord lead to humility:
while he was still an infant, he stayed in a cave, and not even on a bed, but he was laid in a manger of animals;
then he was brought up in the house of Joseph the carpenter and of his mother, who was likewise poor;
and he obeyed his mother and Joseph, and he who is the fountain of wisdom learned, and he asked questions and spoke,
for thus they marveled at his wisdom, it says. He bowed his head to John, and the King received baptism from a servant;
and he did not resist any of those who insulted him, but humbled himself before them as before those more powerful;
And he did not display his ineffable power, but did not resist the mighty of this world;
he stood before the high priest as one condemned; he came before the judge and received judgment;
and he bore the slanders in silence; his face, before which the cherubim tremble, was spat upon by slaves and wretched boys;
then he was given over to death, and to such a death as was reckoned evil among men and worse than all deaths.
Thus he passed through human life from birth to the end, and with such humility.
And at the last he reveals his glory, so that he may glorify with himself those who were humbled with him, the first of whom are those glorious disciples of his,
who ran through the whole world poor and naked, not by wisdom of words, nor by a multitude of servants, nor by an abundance of riches,
but poor and lowly, afflicted on seas and lands, wronged, beaten, persecuted, and at last killed.
These teachings have been given to us as ancestral and divine; let us imitate them, so that out of humility the perfect and true glory of Christ may shine forth for us.
But if you say, "How then may we come to such saving humility and put away from us the evil height of pride?", then hear
that the way of humility is this: that we always seek it and acquire the deeds that lead to it, and despise none of the lowly tasks,
as though we would suffer harm from it; for the soul comes to resemble the work of the body: to whatever its work is directed, to that it draws near, and upon that it is formed.
For this reason I also say to you, brother: let your appearance, your clothing, your walk and your sitting, your food, your bed, your house, and everything
that is in the house, let all of this be lowly and draw toward the side of humility.
Your speech too, your singing, and your dealings with your neighbor: let all of these also be adorned with humility and not with boastfulness.
Do not be boastful and taken up with words of philosophizing, nor with songs of excessive sweetness of voice, nor be one who converses with boastfulness and pride,
but in everything be lowly, gentle toward your neighbor, kind toward your slave, bearing no grudge against those who do evil, loving toward the lowly,
a comforter of the afflicted, a visitor of the sick, despising no one, sweet in word, meek, affable, loved by all, not a praiser of yourself,
nor a lover of praise from others, not a lover of disorderly words, one who conceals your virtues and accuses your own sins.
And do not wait for rebuke from others, so that you may become truly righteous, as it is written:
The righteous man is the accuser of himself, so that you may resemble Job, who was not ashamed before the multitudes of the people to confess his error in their presence.
Do not be harsh in your anger against others, nor be quick and passionate in rebuking, for this too is pride;
Do not be an accuser of your neighbor over his small errors, as though you loved justice beyond measure, but according to the word of the apostle:
"Look to yourself, lest you too be tempted." So be as eager not to be glorified by others as others are eager to be glorified. And remember the word of the Lord,
which says that the praise of men, and doing virtuous deeds before them, is a loss of the reward from God, for it says:
"They have received their reward." But do not bring on yourself that loss through showing off, for God sees all things perfectly.
Therefore I tell you: if you are a lover of glory, love the glory that comes from God, for he gives a splendid reward to all.
And if you have been made worthy of rule and leadership and are glorified by men, become like those
who are under you. If you are a bishop or a father superior, do not exalt yourself over those who are under you,
nor be like the rulers of the world, for the Lord commanded that "whoever wishes to be the eldest shall become the servant of all."
To sum up everything, I have told you in a short word: pursue humility as its lover; love it passionately, so that it may glorify you.
In this way you will attain that true glory of the angels and of God, and Christ will acknowledge you as his own disciple before his angels,
If only you become like the humility of the one who said: "Learn from me,
for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." For his is the glory, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
